title: High-throughput batch inference and embeddings
subtitle: Millions of items through GPUs I own, with the hardware kept busy and the accounting balanced

stats.label: padding waste across the two cards, with zero shape switches
engine cache hit rate, from shape-pure batches
tasks on one GPU over a ten-hour run, zero retries

lede: Offline workloads, synthetic data, extraction, bulk embeddings, are throughput problems, and a serving stack built for chat treats them like chat: padding, idle gaps, producers tied to GPUs for hours, results persisted by whoever is still waiting. I took one model from about 44,000 tokens per second on one NVIDIA Blackwell GPU to a five-minute mean of 163,000 on two NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs without touching a kernel, by building the layers around the engine. Start with From 44K to 163K tokens per second. The first layer is a broker whose unit of scheduling is the token, feeding pull-based workers that stay saturated on mixed hardware. See A message broker that understands tokens.
quote: I did not replace NVIDIA's inference; I fed it.
evidence: High-throughput batch inference: one 7B dense model in FP8 taken from about 44,000 to a five-minute mean of 163,000 tokens per second on two NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs without touching a kernel.
Token-aware scheduling: shape-pure batches packed to each card's four-number contract, with 0.42% padding waste and a 99.9% engine cache hit rate across two mismatched cards.
Distributed systems correctness: done redefined as acknowledged after 6.67 M pending items proved to be 118 K in storage, leaving 12.3 B tokens received and 12.3 B routed.
Inference serving architecture: per-card engine tiers of 524K and 98K tokens per step from one checkpoint, so a slow card slows only itself.
GPU inference optimisation: 4.95 M tasks on one GPU over a ten-hour run with zero retries.
author: Corey James
